Indigenous Health Assessment (Adults 15–54 years)

Medical History

- Current health concerns and risk factors:  2–3-day history of shortness of breath, wheeze and dry cough on exertion; known asthma previously well-controlled. Increased salbutamol use with minimal relief → possible mild asthma exacerbation.  
- Relevant family medical history:  Brother – asthma; sister – eczema.  
- Medications (including OTC or shared medications):  
  • Salbutamol (blue reliever inhaler) – dose/route/frequency not fully documented; currently using PRN up to several times daily.  
  • Clenil (beclomethasone “brown” preventer inhaler) – 3 puffs twice daily; advised to increase to 4 puffs twice daily.  
  • Cetraben cream – dose/route/frequency not documented (skin care).  
  • Hydrocortisone topical cream – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
  • “Flanel Bactroban” mentioned by patient vs “Cetraben” clarified by clinician – conflict noted.  
  • No drug allergies reported; has hay fever (seasonal allergic rhinitis).

Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings: 26-year-old female with established asthma presents with new-onset exertional dyspnoea, wheeze and dry cough for 2–3 days. Salbutamol providing limited relief; preventer inhaler used but due for asthma review. No fever, sputum, chest pain or hospital admissions.

Working diagnosis: Mild asthma exacerbation / loss of control.

Differential diagnoses (consistent with DDx):  
• Asthma exacerbation (High likelihood) – known asthma, classic symptoms, trigger by exercise/allergen, reliever less effective.  
• Viral URTI triggering asthma (Moderate) – acute onset, cough/wheeze without bacterial features.  
• Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction or sub-optimal inhaler technique (Moderate) – symptoms started during running, preventer dose may be inadequate.

Plan:  
• Increase Clenil to 4 puffs twice daily (short-term steroid up-titration).  
• Continue Salbutamol PRN; may use up to every 2 hours.  
• If increasing breathlessness despite reliever, attend Emergency Department.  
• Arrange face-to-face GP appointment within few days for chest exam, peak-flow measurement, inhaler-technique review and consideration of oral steroids/antibiotics if indicated.  
• Provide interim asthma action advice.

Management Plan

- Immediate: patient advised on inhaler dose escalation and red-flag symptoms requiring ED attendance.  
- Follow-up: book in-person GP review in the next few days for assessment and possible further treatment.  
- Education: reinforce asthma action plan, monitor peak flow at home, review preventer adherence.  

Consider:

- Allied health referral (EPC – 10 visits):  Not recorded.  
- Reproductive or sexual health clinic referral:  Not recorded.  
- Mental health support if indicated (e.g., psychologist, AMS support):  Not recorded.  
- CTG registration:  Not recorded.  
- Preventive health follow-up booked (e.g., flu vaccine, Pap test):  Not recorded.  

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Asthma exacerbation – High likelihood. Known asthma, acute wheeze/SOB, increased reliever need, preventer under-dosed.  
2. Viral URTI precipitating asthma – Moderate. Typical time course; no bacterial signs.  
3. Exercise-induced bronchoconstriction/poor inhaler delivery – Moderate. Symptoms began during running; control previously good.

Quality checks

● Missing clinically expected elements: vital signs, physical examination findings, BMI, waist circumference, smoking/alcohol history, immunisation review, mental health screening, cervical screening status, urinalysis.  
● Internal contradictions: Unclear topical medication name (“Flanel Bactroban” vs “Cetraben”) noted.  
● Transcript quality: Mostly clear; some speech overlap and unclear drug names, limiting medication documentation precision.
